Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] CrashStealer 'Werkbit Setup' notarized dropper executes veltod payload
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Fake Apple CrashReporter.app payload running from non-system path · [LLM] CrashStealer LaunchAgent persistence 'com.apple.crashreporter.helper'
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] CrashStealer C2 / exfiltration to Werkbit campaign infrastructure · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] CrashStealer fake password prompt validated via dscl authonly · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
CrashStealer 'Werkbit Setup' notarized dropper executes veltod payload AIDelivery High
Hunts execution of the CrashStealer first-stage dropper: the notarized 'Werkbit Setup' DMG mounts at /Volumes/Werkbit Setup and runs Werkbit.app's executable named 'veltod', which retrieves and launches the stealer. Article-specific because 'veltod' and the Werkbit volume path are unique to this campaign. Rationale: 'veltod' and the '/Volumes/Werkbit Setup/Werkbit.app' path were surfaced from the Jamf write-up (via web search) and are unique campaign strings; a bare process name match is high-fidelity because 'veltod' is not a legitimate binary. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/crashstealer-macos-infostealer-analysis/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/crashstealer-macos-malware-uses.html • https://securityaffairs.com/195278/malware/crashstealer-new-macos-infostealer-uses-signed-apps-to-evade-gatekeeper.html
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1553.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers or SOC analysts detonating the CrashStealer sample in a lab
  • Automated malware sandbox / VirtualTotal detonation hosts inside the fleet
  • A DMG legitimately named 'Werkbit' by an unrelated vendor (none known)
  • Backup/forensic tooling replaying the mounted volume path
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 of veltod and the parent process; confirm the binary launched from /Volumes/Werkbit Setup and check the mounted DMG origin (browser Downloads, quarantine xattr, originating URL). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the veltod process tree, unmount the Werkbit volume and quarantine the DMG; block werkbit.io at the proxy. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for CrashReporter.app creation, the com.apple.crashreporter.helper LaunchAgent, dscl authonly credential validation, and outbound traffic to 179.43.166.242 / icky-lyrical.com.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "veltod"
   or FolderPath has "/Volumes/Werkbit Setup/"
   or FolderPath endswith "/Werkbit.app/Contents/MacOS/veltod"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "/Volumes/Werkbit Setup/"
   or TargetProcessName endswith "/Werkbit.app/Contents/MacOS/veltod"
   or TargetProcessName endswith "/veltod"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, Hash
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fake Apple CrashReporter.app payload running from non-system path AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the CrashStealer second-stage payload masquerading as Apple's crash reporter: a CrashReporter.app bundle (bundle id com.apple.crashreporter) executing from a user-writable location rather than the macOS system path. Legitimate macOS crash reporting is ReportCrash under /System, so a user-space CrashReporter.app is anomalous. Rationale: Article + Jamf confirm the payload impersonates Apple's crash reporter with bundle id com.apple.crashreporter and name CrashReporter.app; genuine Apple crash reporting is ReportCrash under /System, so any user-space CrashReporter.app is high-signal masquerading. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/crashstealer-macos-infostealer-analysis/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/macos-stealer-mimics-apples-crash-report/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1036.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A third-party crash-analytics tool coincidentally bundling a 'CrashReporter.app' in an app's Contents (rare)
  • Developer test builds copying a CrashReporter helper into ~/Library
  • Backup/restore tooling touching a stored CrashReporter.app path
  • Sample detonation in a research VM
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("/Library/Developer/", "Xcode") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the CrashReporter.app executable, inspect its code-signing identity (expect self/re-signed, not Apple) and parent process; confirm path is user-writable. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the process, quarantine the bundle, and preserve the LaunchAgent plist. 3) Hunt: correlate with veltod dropper execution, com.apple.crashreporter.helper persistence, dscl authonly prompts, and C2 beacons to the known infra.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "/CrashReporter.app/"
| where not (FolderPath startswith "/System/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "/CrashReporter.app/"
| where not (TargetProcessName startswith "/System/")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, Hash
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CrashStealer LaunchAgent persistence 'com.apple.crashreporter.helper' AIInstallation High
Detects creation of the CrashStealer persistence LaunchAgent plist impersonating an Apple label. The malware writes a LaunchAgent named com.apple.crashreporter.helper into a LaunchAgents directory; this exact label is not a legitimate Apple artifact (real crash reporting uses com.apple.ReportCrash). Rationale: The LaunchAgent label 'com.apple.crashreporter.helper' is stated verbatim in the article and is a masquerade — legitimate Apple crash reporting persists as com.apple.ReportCrash, making the exact label a near-zero-FP artifact. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/crashstealer-macos-infostealer-analysis/ • https://www.itnews.com.au/news/apple-notarised-crashstealer-malware-poses-as-macos-crash-reporting-app-627340
ATT&CKT1543.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An admin or EDR tool re-writing the plist during remediation testing
  • Forensic imaging replaying a captured LaunchAgents directory
  • Security researcher recreating the persistence in a lab
  • Backup restore repopulating ~/Library/LaunchAgents
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the plist Program/ProgramArguments to find the payload path and the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName); hash the referenced binary. 2) Contain: isolate host, unload the LaunchAgent (launchctl bootout) and quarantine both the plist and the referenced executable. 3) Hunt: pivot to the writing process (expect CrashReporter.app/veltod), and sweep the fleet for the same plist name and for C2 beacons to 179.43.166.242 / icky-lyrical.com.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has "/Library/LaunchAgents"
| where FileName has "com.apple.crashreporter.helper"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileCreate")
| where TargetFilePath has "/Library/LaunchAgents"
| where TargetFileName has "com.apple.crashreporter.helper"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CrashStealer fake password prompt validated via dscl authonly AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the CrashStealer credential-capture step: after showing a fake macOS admin password prompt, the malware validates the entered password locally with 'dscl ... authonly' to unlock the Keychain. Surfaces dscl authonly invocations and their parent process so analysts can spot GUI-prompt-driven credential theft. Rationale: Article states CrashStealer validates the fake-prompt password with dscl and 'authonly' is the sub-command that performs local auth; pairing the dscl binary with authonly plus surfacing the parent process is the article-specific credential-capture signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/crashstealer-macos-infostealer-analysis/ • https://appleinsider.com/articles/26/07/13/crashstealer-malware-poses-as-an-apple-tool-to-steal-passwords-mac-data
ATT&CKT1056.002 T1555.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • MDM / Jamf tooling verifying a user's local password during enrollment or policy checks
  • Admin scripts that test credentials before a privileged operation
  • Self-service password-change utilities invoking dscl authonly
  • SSO/keychain helper tools performing local auth checks
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("jamf","authorizationhost","SecurityAgent","managementclient") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "/Library/Application Support/JAMF/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the parent process of dscl — a masquerading CrashReporter.app/veltod parent is malicious, an MDM agent (jamf, authorizationhost) is likely benign. 2) Contain: if parent is untrusted, isolate the host, kill the tree, and force-rotate the user's login/Keychain-protected credentials. 3) Hunt: correlate with the fake CrashReporter.app process, LaunchAgent persistence, browser/wallet file access, and outbound C2 to the known infrastructure.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "dscl"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "authonly"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith "/dscl"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "authonly"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CrashStealer C2 / exfiltration to Werkbit campaign infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Detects host communication with confirmed CrashStealer command-and-control and delivery infrastructure — C2 IP 179.43.166.242 and the shared backend / lookalike-meeting domains (icky-lyrical.com, endpoint-api-v1.com, werkbit.io, cohezo.io/.com, cordinex.io). CrashStealer exfiltrates AES-256-GCM-encrypted ZIPs over libcurl to this infra. Rationale: C2 IP 179.43.166.242 and the campaign domains come from the article's pre-extracted IOCs, with icky-lyrical.com independently confirmed by Jamf/SecurityAffairs as the shared backend; direct IOC matches on confirmed C2 are inherently high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/crashstealer-macos-infostealer-analysis/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195278/malware/crashstealer-new-macos-infostealer-uses-signed-apps-to-evade-gatekeeper.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel scanners / sandboxes in the fleet resolving the IOC domains for analysis
  • A security researcher visiting werkbit.io from a corporate host
  • Passive DNS/URL-scanning browser extensions pre-fetching the domains
  • Sinkhole or takedown infrastructure now resolving the domains
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process (expect CrashReporter.app/veltod/libcurl-linked binary) and whether a preceding hidden ZIP was created in the user profile; confirm outbound bytes suggest exfil. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block 179.43.166.242 and all listed domains at proxy/DNS, and treat all local Keychain/browser/wallet credentials as compromised — force rotation. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for any resolution of these domains, for the veltod dropper, and for the com.apple.crashreporter.helper LaunchAgent.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "179.43.166.242"
   or RemoteUrl has_any ("werkbit.io","endpoint-api-v1.com","icky-lyrical.com","cohezo.io","cohezo.com","cordinex.io")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "179.43.166.242"
   or DstHostname has_any ("werkbit.io","endpoint-api-v1.com","icky-lyrical.com","cohezo.io","cohezo.com","cordinex.io")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest

DIRAC is vulnerable to RCE in FileCatalog DatasetManager via SQL injection + eval

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] DIRAC FileCatalog/Tornado service spawns shell or recon binary (CVE-2026-61667 eval RCE)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] DIRAC dirac.cfg secrets read via shell utility (post-RCE credential access) · [LLM] DIRAC log evidence removal under /opt/dirac (post-RCE anti-forensics)
DIRAC FileCatalog/Tornado service spawns shell or recon binary (CVE-2026-61667 eval RCE) AIExploitation High
Hunts the RCE landing for CVE-2026-61667: the DIRAC FileCatalog DatasetManager passes SQL-injection-controlled data into eval(), so the DIRAC service Python process (Tornado/dirac-service under /opt/dirac) executing an attacker payload will spawn a shell or recon/download binary. A DIRAC data service should never fork /bin/sh, id, whoami, curl or nc, making the parent→child pair high-fidelity. Rationale: Anchors on the DIRAC service invocation strings (tornado-start-all, DataManagement/FileCatalog, TornadoFileCatalogHandler, dirac-service) and /opt/dirac runtime path confirmed in DIRAC docs, paired with a shell/recon child set — the exact behaviour of an eval() RCE landing. Cross-checked GHSA + GitLab advisory mirror; DIRAC HTTPS/Tornado service docs confirm the handler path and /opt/dirac supervision. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m4m7-4cw8-62j6 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/dirac/CVE-2026-61667/ • https://dirac.readthedocs.io/en/latest/AdministratorGuide/ServerInstallations/HTTPSServices.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DIRAC agent/service legitimately shelling out to curl/wget to fetch CA CRLs or CVMFS content
  • Admin-invoked health-check or monitoring plugin running under the dirac service tree
  • Backup or housekeeping cron launched from the DIRAC runit environment calling sh/bash
  • DIRAC pilot/job wrappers invoking id/hostname during environment setup
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("crl","cvmfs","/ca/","cern.ch"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full process tree for the flagged child — confirm the parent is the FileCatalog/Tornado Python process and inspect the child command line for reverse-shell, download, or recon intent; correlate with FileCatalog service access logs for a preceding checkDataset call. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the offending process tree, and rotate everything the DIRAC service can reach — dirac.cfg DB credentials, all stored proxies and tokens — since RCE implies full secret exposure. Step 3 (hunt): Search the same host and peer DIRAC servers for reads of dirac.cfg, proxy/token exfiltration, and log tampering (UCs 2 and 3); verify DIRAC is patched to 8.0.79 / 9.0.22 / 9.1.10.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "/opt/dirac/"
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("tornado-start-all","DataManagement/FileCatalog","dirac-service","TornadoFileCatalogHandler")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","perl")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| extend ChildName = tostring(split(TargetProcessName, "/")[-1])
| where ActingProcessName startswith "/opt/dirac/"
    or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("tornado-start-all","DataManagement/FileCatalog","dirac-service","TornadoFileCatalogHandler")
| where ChildName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","perl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ChildName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: DIRAC FileCatalog Service Spawns Shell or Recon Binary
id: 6f2a1d4e-9c3b-4a1e-8f7d-2b5c0e1a7d33
description: Detects the DIRAC FileCatalog/Tornado service process (under /opt/dirac) spawning a shell or recon/download binary, consistent with CVE-2026-61667 eval-based RCE.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m4m7-4cw8-62j6
  - https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/dirac/CVE-2026-61667/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/14
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1059.004
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  parent:
    ParentImage|startswith: '/opt/dirac/'
  parent_cmd:
    ParentCommandLine|contains:
      - 'tornado-start-all'
      - 'DataManagement/FileCatalog'
      - 'dirac-service'
      - 'TornadoFileCatalogHandler'
  child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/sh'
      - '/bash'
      - '/dash'
      - '/zsh'
      - '/id'
      - '/whoami'
      - '/uname'
      - '/hostname'
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'
      - '/nc'
      - '/ncat'
      - '/perl'
  condition: (parent or parent_cmd) and child
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @user.name:dirac @process.name:(sh OR bash OR dash OR zsh OR id OR whoami OR uname OR hostname OR curl OR wget OR nc OR ncat OR perl)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentImageFileName=/\/opt\/dirac\//i OR ParentBaseFileName=/(tornado|dirac)/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(sh|bash|dash|zsh|id|whoami|uname|hostname|curl|wget|nc|ncat|perl)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as process values(Processes.process_path) as process_path from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_path="/opt/dirac/*" OR Processes.parent_process="*tornado-start-all*" OR Processes.parent_process="*DataManagement/FileCatalog*" OR Processes.parent_process="*dirac-service*" OR Processes.parent_process="*TornadoFileCatalogHandler*") (Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","perl")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as process values(Processes.process_path) as process_path from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_path="/opt/dirac/*" OR Processes.parent_process="*tornado-start-all*" OR Processes.parent_process="*DataManagement/FileCatalog*" OR Processes.parent_process="*dirac-service*" OR Processes.parent_process="*TornadoFileCatalogHandler*") (Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","perl")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
DIRAC dirac.cfg secrets read via shell utility (post-RCE credential access) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the credential-harvesting step called out in CVE-2026-61667: after RCE the attacker reads /opt/dirac/etc/dirac.cfg to obtain database passwords. Legitimately dirac.cfg is only parsed by the DIRAC Python runtime, so a cat/grep/less/strings process whose command line references dirac.cfg is a strong indicator of manual secret theft. Rationale: dirac.cfg is named in the advisory as the file holding DB passwords; it is normally read only by the DIRAC Python runtime, so an interactive reader binary referencing it is a precise credential-theft signal with minimal legitimate use. Second-sourced via the GitLab advisory mirror. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m4m7-4cw8-62j6 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/dirac/CVE-2026-61667/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DIRAC administrator manually inspecting or grepping dirac.cfg during troubleshooting
  • Config-management/backup tooling (cp/scp) copying dirac.cfg as part of host provisioning
  • Ops runbook using strings/cat to diff configuration between DIRAC nodes
  • Site packaging scripts templating dirac.cfg with sed
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ansible","puppet","salt-minion","cfengine") or FileName in~ ("cp","scp") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cron","crond"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating user and parent process — if the reader was spawned from the FileCatalog/Tornado service tree (UC1) rather than an interactive admin session, treat as confirmed theft. Step 2 (contain): Immediately rotate every credential in dirac.cfg (database passwords, connection secrets) and force re-issuance of any proxies/tokens managed by this instance; isolate the host. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the same host for outbound transfer of the config (scp/curl uploads), proxy/token DB dumps, and evidence removal (UC3); check whether the same account read dirac.cfg on other DIRAC servers.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "dirac.cfg"
| where FileName in~ ("cat","grep","egrep","zgrep","less","more","head","tail","awk","sed","strings","xxd","od","vi","vim","nano","cp","scp","base64")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| extend ChildName = tostring(split(TargetProcessName, "/")[-1])
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "dirac.cfg"
| where ChildName in~ ("cat","grep","egrep","zgrep","less","more","head","tail","awk","sed","strings","xxd","od","vi","vim","nano","cp","scp","base64")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ChildName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DIRAC log evidence removal under /opt/dirac (post-RCE anti-forensics) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the log-tampering step the advisory notes an attacker can perform after RCE ('remove evidence of the exploit from the log'). Detects rm/shred/truncate/unlink/sed targeting files under the DIRAC install tree's log directories, excluding the legitimate svlogd/logrotate rotation processes. Rationale: Uses the advisory's explicit note that an attacker can remove exploit evidence from local logs, anchored to the /opt/dirac install tree confirmed in DIRAC docs and scoped to destructive utilities while excluding the svlogd/logrotate rotation that legitimately manages DIRAC logs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m4m7-4cw8-62j6 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/dirac/CVE-2026-61667/ • https://dirac.readthedocs.io/en/latest/AdministratorGuide/ServerInstallations/HTTPSServices.html
ATT&CKT1070.004 T1070.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin manually clearing stuck/oversized DIRAC service logs during maintenance
  • Custom cleanup cron pruning old /opt/dirac/runit log directories
  • DIRAC upgrade/reinstall scripts removing prior version log trees
  • Disk-space remediation runbooks truncating verbose component logs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("logrotate","svlogd","dirac-install","install_site")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Determine what was deleted/truncated and by which user and parent process; if the deleting process descends from the FileCatalog/Tornado service tree or a shell spawned by it (UC1), treat as anti-forensics. Step 2 (contain): Preserve remaining logs and disk artifacts (snapshot the volume), isolate the host, and pull any centrally-forwarded copies of the destroyed DIRAC logs before they age out. Step 3 (hunt): Reconstruct the timeline from surviving central logs — look for the preceding FileCatalog checkDataset request, shell spawn (UC1), and dirac.cfg/secret access (UC2) on this and peer DIRAC nodes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("rm","shred","truncate","unlink","sed")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/opt/dirac/" and ProcessCommandLine has "log"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("svlogd","logrotate")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| extend ChildName = tostring(split(TargetProcessName, "/")[-1]), ParentName = tostring(split(ActingProcessName, "/")[-1])
| where ChildName in~ ("rm","shred","truncate","unlink","sed")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "/opt/dirac/" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "log"
| where ParentName !in~ ("svlogd","logrotate")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ChildName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CrashStealer macOS Malware Uses Notarized Dropper to Pass Gatekeeper Checks

The Hacker News
2026-07-13 9 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have flagged a new macOS information stealer called CrashStealer that's capable of harvesting sensitive data from compromised systems. Unlike other information stealers that are built on AppleScript droppers or Objective-C-based wrappers, CrashStealer is implemented in native C++, according to Jamf Threat Labs. Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] CrashStealer 'veltod' dropper execution from mounted Werkbit.app DMG

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] CrashStealer C2 pull: veltod fetching sys.cache from GitHub + endpoint-api-v1.com · Network connections to article IPs / domains

CrashStealer 'veltod' dropper execution from mounted Werkbit.app DMG AIDelivery High
Hunts execution of the notarized CrashStealer first-stage binary 'veltod' (bundle dev.golove.velto) launched from a mounted Werkbit.app disk image. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact malicious executable name and the /Volumes-mounted Werkbit.app container that clears Gatekeeper via the revoked Emil Grigorov (WWB7JA7AQV) Developer ID. Rationale: Anchors on the exact first-stage executable name 'veltod' and the /Volumes-mounted Werkbit.app container named in the article and confirmed by Jamf (bundle dev.golove.velto). Renaming 'veltod' is caught by the Werkbit.app path clause. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/crashstealer-macos-infostealer-analysis/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-crashstealer-malware-poses-as-apple-crash-reporting-tool/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195278/malware/crashstealer-new-macos-infostealer-uses-signed-apps-to-evade-gatekeeper.html
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1553.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal tool coincidentally binary-named 'veltod' (extremely unlikely, non-dictionary name)
  • QA/malware-analysis workstation intentionally detonating the sample from a mounted DMG
  • Security researcher re-mounting a captured Werkbit.app for analysis
  • EDR sensor replaying archived process events during backfill
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("mdworker","XProtect","VirusTotal")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the process image path is under /Volumes/Werkbit* or */Werkbit.app/* and pull the code-signing identity — Apple revoked the Emil Grigorov (WWB7JA7AQV) cert, so a valid-but-revoked signature confirms the sample. Note the mount source DMG and downloading user. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the veltod PID, unmount and quarantine the DMG, and force-expire the user's browser/keychain sessions. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the host for a /tmp/CrashReporter.dmg drop, a new ~/Library/LaunchAgents plist, and outbound traffic to 179.43.166.242 or endpoint-api-v1.com to scope full-chain compromise.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "veltod"
   or (FolderPath has "Werkbit.app" and FolderPath has "/Volumes/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

CrashStealer C2 pull: veltod fetching sys.cache from GitHub + endpoint-api-v1.com AICommand & Control High
Hunts the CrashStealer second-stage retrieval where 'veltod' pulls 'sys.cache' from github/raw.githubusercontent.com (mgothiclove/pkeys) and the shell downloader reaches the delivery endpoint endpoint-api-v1[.]com/d/f1b24e, plus sibling campaign domains. Article-specific via the exact attacker-controlled domains and the anomalous veltod->GitHub egress. Rationale: endpoint-api-v1.com, cohezo.io/.com, cordinex.io and werkbit.io are attacker-registered domains confirmed by Jamf; the veltod->raw.githubusercontent.com clause catches the mgothiclove/pkeys dead-drop pull that legitimate software never performs. High fidelity because these domains have no benign use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/crashstealer-macos-infostealer-analysis/ • https://appleinsider.com/articles/26/07/13/crashstealer-malware-poses-as-an-apple-tool-to-steal-passwords-mac-data
ATT&CKT1105 T1102.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment or sandbox tooling actively resolving the IOC domains during analysis
  • Passive-DNS or scanner appliance sweeping the campaign domains
  • A benign process on the host querying github; note the detection requires veltod as the initiator for github, so this is filtered
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ logging the blocked resolution (still worth reviewing)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the resolving host and the initiating process; confirm whether the query is for a hardcoded campaign domain (endpoint-api-v1.com etc.) versus the veltod->github dead-drop. Check if resolution succeeded and any follow-on connection to 179.43.166.242. Step 2 (contain): Sinkhole/block the campaign domains and 179.43.166.242 at egress, isolate the host if veltod or CrashReporter is present. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all endpoints for the same domain resolutions and for /tmp/CrashReporter.dmg and LaunchAgent persistence to find other PIN-gated victims.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("endpoint-api-v1.com","cohezo.io","cohezo.com","cordinex.io","werkbit.io")
   or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "veltod" and RemoteUrl has_any ("raw.githubusercontent.com","github.com"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,

| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity

| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, DstIpAddr, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CrashStealer second-stage payload CrashReporter.dmg staged in /tmp AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of the CrashStealer next-stage disk image 'CrashReporter.dmg' in /tmp (macOS /private/tmp) by the shell downloader script. Article-specific via the exact staged payload filename and temp-directory drop path that the veltod-invoked curl chain uses. Rationale: CrashReporter.dmg written to /tmp is the exact staged payload filename and path named in the article; a disk image landing in a world-writable temp dir from a downloader script is a high-signal, near-zero-benign event on macOS endpoints. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/crashstealer-macos-infostealer-analysis/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/crashstealer-macos-malware-uses.html
ATT&CKT1105 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer/CI job coincidentally building a disk image literally named CrashReporter.dmg into /tmp (rare; verify signer)
  • Crash-diagnostics tooling exporting an archive to tmp (would not typically be a .dmg named CrashReporter)
  • Malware-analysis lab detonating the sample
  • Backup/temp cleanup tools moving a previously dropped payload
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the writing process — a curl/sh/bash chain parented by veltod strongly confirms CrashStealer; capture the file hash and the source URL (endpoint-api-v1.com/d/f1b24e). Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, quarantine /tmp/CrashReporter.dmg before it is mounted/executed, and terminate any veltod or downloader shell. Step 3 (hunt): Look for a mounted CrashReporter volume, a new LaunchAgent plist, keychain/browser credential access, and egress to 179.43.166.242.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName =~ "CrashReporter.dmg"
| where FolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/private/tmp/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

CrashStealer LaunchAgent persistence written by temp/DMG-resident process AIInstallation Medium
Hunts CrashStealer establishing persistence by writing a LaunchAgent plist into ~/Library/LaunchAgents from a process running out of /tmp, /private/tmp or a mounted /Volumes DMG (the CrashReporter/veltod stager that copies and re-signs itself). Article-specific via the temp/DMG-resident initiator writing the autostart plist. Rationale: Anchors LaunchAgent persistence (T1543.001) to the CrashStealer-specific initiator context — a stager running from /tmp, /private/tmp or a mounted DMG, or literally named veltod/CrashReporter — which separates it from the thousands of legitimate installers that also write LaunchAgents. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/crashstealer-macos-infostealer-analysis/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/macos-malware-apple-crash-reporter/
ATT&CKT1543.001 T1553.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A software installer temporarily extracting a helper into /private/tmp before registering a legitimate LaunchAgent
  • App run directly from a mounted DMG that installs its own auto-launch helper (e.g. some updater tools)
  • Homebrew/pkg post-install scripts writing agents from a temp working dir
  • MDM/config-management pushing a LaunchAgent via a staged temp payload
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("installer","package_script_service","munki","jamf") )
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Open the new plist and read the Program/ProgramArguments — a path pointing at a copied+re-signed CrashStealer binary (often in ~/Library or /tmp) confirms it; check the code signature (valid but revoked = CrashStealer). Step 2 (contain): Unload and delete the LaunchAgent (launchctl bootout), remove the referenced binary, isolate host. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate with a preceding /tmp/CrashReporter.dmg drop, codesign invocations with -f/--force by the stager, and egress to 179.43.166.242 to confirm the full chain.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has "/Library/LaunchAgents/"
| where FileName endswith ".plist"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/private/tmp/","/Volumes/")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veltod","CrashReporter")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceFileEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath has "/Library/LaunchAgents/"
| where FileName endswith ".plist"
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/private/tmp/","/Volumes/")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veltod","CrashReporter")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CrashStealer credential harvest: temp/DMG process reading keychain + browser/wallet stores AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the CrashStealer collection stage where a process running from /tmp, /private/tmp or a mounted DMG accesses the login keychain and Chromium/Firefox credential databases (Login Data, Cookies, key4.db, logins.json) plus wallet Local Extension Settings. Article-specific via the temp/DMG-resident non-browser initiator touching multiple credential stores. Rationale: CrashStealer harvests browsers, wallets, password managers and the login keychain; anchoring on a non-browser process from /tmp/DMG touching >=2 distinct credential stores (keychain + Chromium Login Data/Cookies/Firefox key4.db + wallet extension storage) yields a fan-out signal that legitimate single-app access does not produce. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/crashstealer-macos-infostealer-analysis/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/macos-stealer-mimics-apples-crash-report/
ATT&CKT1555.001 T1555.003 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate password manager or browser-import utility bulk-reading credential stores (filtered by excluding browser initiators and requiring a temp/DMG initiator)
  • Backup software (e.g. Time Machine helper) enumerating ~/Library
  • Forensic/DFIR collection tooling run from a mounted volume
  • Security product scanning keychain and browser profiles
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("1Password","Bitwarden","KeePassXC","backupd","mds","mdworker_shared")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process and its path — a binary in /tmp or a mounted DMG (or named veltod/CrashReporter) reading login.keychain-db plus multiple browser stores confirms active harvesting. Note which browsers/wallets were touched. Step 2 (contain): Isolate host, kill the process, and force credential rotation for the affected user: keychain/login password, browser-saved passwords, and any crypto wallet seed phrases immediately (assume wallet drain risk). Step 3 (hunt): Look for a subsequent ZIP archive written to a temp dir and outbound transfer to 179.43.166.242; scope other hosts for the same fan-out pattern.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/tmp/","/private/tmp/","/Volumes/")
   or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veltod","CrashReporter")
| where FileName in~ ("login.keychain-db","Login Data","Cookies","key4.db","logins.json")
   or FolderPath has_any ("/Local Extension Settings/","/Application Support/Exodus/","/Application Support/Ledger Live/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Google Chrome","firefox","Brave Browser","Microsoft Edge","com.apple.WebKit")
| summarize DistinctStores = dcount(FileName), Stores = make_set(FileName, 20),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| where DistinctStores >= 2   // >=2 distinct credential stores by one temp/DMG process = harvest fan-out
| order by LastSeen desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.

// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).

CrashStealer AES-GCM ZIP exfiltration to 179.43.166.242 over libcurl AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the CrashStealer exfiltration stage: outbound connection to the hardcoded attacker C2 179.43.166[.]242, which received the AES-GCM-encrypted ZIP of harvested browser/wallet/keychain data over libcurl. Article-specific via the exact C2 IP confirmed by Jamf (previously leaked in the app's ATS plist exception). Rationale: 179.43.166.242 is the hardcoded exfiltration C2 confirmed by Jamf (leaked via an ATS exception in an earlier build's plist) and reported by The Hacker News; any endpoint connecting to this IP is a direct data-theft indicator with essentially no benign use. Cross-checked against: • https://www.jamf.com/blog/crashstealer-macos-infostealer-analysis/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195278/malware/crashstealer-new-macos-infostealer-uses-signed-apps-to-evade-gatekeeper.html
ATT&CKT1041 T1560.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel or scanning infrastructure probing the C2 IP
  • A researcher/sandbox intentionally connecting to the IP for analysis
  • Shared-hosting reuse where the IP later serves benign content (verify timing vs. campaign window)
  • Proxy/NAT egress that aggregates many hosts behind one source — confirm the true internal originator
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the internal host and initiating process connecting to 179.43.166.242 and measure bytes_out — a spike indicates the ZIP was exfiltrated. Correlate with prior credential-store access on the same host. Step 2 (contain): Block 179.43.166.242 at the perimeter, isolate the host, and treat all local credentials (keychain, browser passwords, crypto wallet seeds, password-manager vaults) as compromised — rotate immediately. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all endpoints for connections to this IP and the campaign domains (endpoint-api-v1.com, cohezo.io/.com, cordinex.io, werkbit.io), and for the CrashReporter.dmg/LaunchAgent artifacts to enumerate the full victim set.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "179.43.166.242"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "179.43.166.242"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort,
          RequestURL, SentBytes, ReceivedBytes, ApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] DIRAC ReqManager service (CVE-2026-45579) spawning a shell or recon/egress binary
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] DIRAC post-exploit read of dirac.cfg by a shell/read utility (CVE-2026-45579 credential theft)
DIRAC ReqManager service (CVE-2026-45579) spawning a shell or recon/egress binary AIExploitation High
Hunts the RCE payload executing: the DIRAC RequestManager service (a Python DB-facing handler launched via dirac-service/dirac-tornado as ReqManager/TornadoReqManager) spawning /bin/sh, bash or a recon/egress tool. The eval() on the unrecognised groupingAttribute walks back to the os module, so successful exploitation manifests as this DB service forking a shell — something ReqManager never does legitimately (unlike RequestExecutingAgent, which forks a ProcessPool). Rationale: Anchored on the ReqManager/ReqManagerHandler/dirac-service parent identity (DIRAC docs: ReqManager is the DB-facing handler that never shells out) combined with any shell/recon/egress child — the exact tree the eval()->os.* chain from the advisory produces. Parent token deliberately excludes RequestExecutingAgent, which forks a legitimate ProcessPool. Datadog/Falcon left empty: their provided auditd/ProcessRollup2 schemas expose no parent command line to key the DIRAC-service parent on (only ParentBaseFileName='python', too generic). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/dirac/CVE-2026-45579/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9jpv-c7p4-997x • https://dirac.diracgrid.org/en/latest/AdministratorGuide/Systems/RequestManagement/rmsComponents.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DIRAC administrator running diagnostic shell commands under the runit/supervisor process tree during service troubleshooting
  • Container entrypoint/init wrapper spawning a shell during a dirac-service (re)start
  • Config-management (Ansible/Puppet/Salt) restarting dirac-tornado and running post-restart health-check shell hooks
  • Site monitoring probes (monit/nagios) that shell out from the service supervisor
  • A local health-check script using curl/nc to poll the ReqManager port on service start
Suppression filter
| where ChildCmd !has "healthcheck" and ChildCmd !has "/opt/dirac/pro/versions" and ChildCmd !has "runsvdir"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child command line and SHA256; correlate against the ReqManager log for the exception traceback the advisory says the exploit leaves (NameError/AttributeError referencing 'Request.' or dunder strings such as __class__/__globals__/__builtins__), and identify the authenticated user whose RPC to getRequestCountersWeb preceded it. 2) Contain: isolate the DIRAC host, rotate all secrets in dirac.cfg (database passwords) and revoke every stored proxy/token, then upgrade DIRAC to 8.0.79 / 9.0.22 / 9.1.10. 3) Hunt: search the same host for reads of dirac.cfg by non-DIRAC processes, outbound egress from the service, and truncation/deletion of the RequestManager log (evidence removal noted in the advisory).

| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("dirac-service","dirac-tornado","ReqManagerHandler","ReqManager")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","id","whoami","hostname","uname","cat","base64","chmod")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("dirac-service","dirac-tornado","ReqManagerHandler","ReqManager")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","/ksh","/curl","/wget","/nc","/ncat","/socat","/id","/whoami","/hostname","/uname","/cat","/base64","/chmod")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DIRAC post-exploit read of dirac.cfg by a shell/read utility (CVE-2026-45579 credential theft) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the credential-theft step the advisory describes: after the eval() RCE, the attacker reads the local dirac.cfg to harvest database passwords and export stored proxies/tokens. Keys on a read/exfil utility (cat, grep, base64, curl, etc.) whose own command line references dirac.cfg — excluding the Python DIRAC service that carries dirac.cfg as a legitimate --cfg argument. Rationale: Keys on dirac.cfg (the file the advisory names as holding DB passwords and gating proxy/token export) appearing in the command line of a read/exfil utility rather than the Python service. The reader-binary allowlist excludes the legitimate DIRAC process, which carries dirac.cfg as a --cfg argument — so any cat/grep/base64/curl of dirac.cfg is anomalous. Portable across all process-telemetry platforms because it keys on the executing process's own command line. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/dirac/CVE-2026-45579/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9jpv-c7p4-997x
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DIRAC administrator manually running cat/grep on dirac.cfg during troubleshooting over SSH
  • Backup jobs (tar/rsync driven via cat) reading the DIRAC etc/ directory
  • Config-management tooling templating or diffing dirac.cfg on each run
  • Monitoring/inventory scripts grepping dirac.cfg for a version or option value
  • Site install/upgrade scripts copying dirac.cfg with scp/curl to a new node
Suppression filter
and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("dirac-service","dirac-tornado","ReqManagerHandler","ReqManager")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent of the reader process — if it descends from the DIRAC service (dirac-service/dirac-tornado/ReqManager) rather than an interactive admin shell, treat as confirmed exploitation; check whether the command pipes to base64/curl/nc (exfil) and whether stored proxy/token files were touched. 2) Contain: isolate the host, immediately rotate every credential in dirac.cfg and revoke all stored user proxies and tokens, and patch DIRAC to 8.0.79 / 9.0.22 / 9.1.10. 3) Hunt: pivot on the authenticated user who called getRequestCountersWeb, review the ReqManager log for the eval exception traceback, and look for outbound transfers of dirac.cfg / proxy material and any subsequent log truncation.

| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "dirac.cfg"
| where FileName in~ ("cat","grep","egrep","less","more","head","tail","base64","od","strings","xxd","curl","wget","scp","nc","ncat")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "dirac.cfg"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/cat","/grep","/egrep","/less","/more","/head","/tail","/base64","/od","/strings","/xxd","/curl","/wget","/scp","/nc","/ncat")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Google and Microsoft Pull ModHeader With 1.6 Million Installs After Dormant Collector Found

The Hacker News
2026-07-13 8 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Google and Microsoft have pulled ModHeader, a popular header-editing extension with roughly 1.6 million installs across Chrome and Edge, after researchers found a hidden browsing-history collector built into its official store version. The collector was dormant. An empty allow-list kept it switched off, and no proof has emerged that it ever gathered or sent a single browsing domain. The

ATT&CKT1176 T1190 T1195.002 T1539
Domainsstanfordstudies.com api.stanfordstudies.com extensions-hub.com
IPs3.147.61.167

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Trojanised ModHeader extension ID (idgpnmonknjnojddfkpgkljpfnnfcklj) present on host · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ModHeader collector callback to stanfordstudies.com / extensions-hub.com · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] ModHeader browsing-history exfil POST to api.stanfordstudies.com/app/log · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
ModHeader collector callback to stanfordstudies.com / extensions-hub.com AICommand & Control High
Hunts host resolution and network connections to the two domains hardwired into the trojanised ModHeader extension: extensions-hub.com (pinged on install/update/uninstall, confirmed active) and api.stanfordstudies.com (the dormant daily browsing-history exfil endpoint). Because the browser process itself makes the call, the connection is attributed to chrome.exe/msedge.exe. Rationale: Both domains are named directly in the article and corroborated by Yunus Aydın and HackIndex teardowns; extensions-hub.com fires on every install/update/uninstall (confirmed active), making this a reliable trip-wire even though the browsing-history exfil path is gated off. Cross-checked against: • https://aydinnyunus.github.io/2026/07/12/modheader-data-exfiltration-stanfordstudies/ • https://hackindex.io/research/modheader-malware-chrome-spyware • https://gbhackers.com/modheader-chrome-extension-exposes-900000-users/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1176
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately-registered but similarly-named advertising domain sharing the extensions-hub.com string in a subdomain
  • Security researchers or the SOC intentionally detonating the sample in a sandbox VM
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling actively resolving the IOC domains for verdict lookups
  • A proxy/DNS-security appliance's own IOC-testing beacon
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm InitiatingProcessFileName is a browser (chrome.exe/msedge.exe) and check whether the host has the ModHeader extension ID idgpnmonknjnojddfkpgkljpfnnfcklj on disk (see the extension-inventory UC). 2) CONTAIN: Block stanfordstudies.com and extensions-hub.com at DNS and proxy; push removal of the ModHeader extension and verify no managed-extension policy / profile-sync will reinstall it. 3) HUNT: If the host also beaconed to api.stanfordstudies.com/app/log, treat the collector as activated — pull proxy logs for the POST body size and rotate any API keys / bearer tokens / session cookies the user pasted into ModHeader's header history.

| where RemoteUrl has_any ("stanfordstudies.com", "extensions-hub.com")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Connections=count(), SampleUrl=any(RemoteUrl) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP
| order by LastSeen desc
ImDnsActivity

| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Queries=count() by SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, DnsQuery
| order by LastSeen desc

Trojanised ModHeader extension ID (idgpnmonknjnojddfkpgkljpfnnfcklj) present on host AIInstallation High
Inventories hosts where the pulled ModHeader extension is (or was) installed by matching its Chrome/Edge Web Store extension ID in the on-disk extension directory. This finds the affected population regardless of whether the dormant collector ever fired, so you can drive removal and secret-rotation. Rationale: The extension ID idgpnmonknjnojddfkpgkljpfnnfcklj is the single most durable IOC in the article — it is fixed, unique to the pulled build, and appears in the browser's on-disk extension directory whether or not the collector activated, giving a clean affected-host inventory. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/google-and-microsoft-pull-modheader.html • https://hackindex.io/research/modheader-malware-chrome-spyware • https://blog.gridinsoft.com/modheader-malware/
ATT&CKT1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • This ID is unique to the pulled ModHeader build, so true FPs are near-zero; a benign hit would be a security team staging the sample for analysis
  • Backup/EDR agents copying an existing extension directory during imaging (path still confirms exposure)
  • A forensic image being mounted/scanned on an analyst workstation
  • Roaming-profile sync replaying the folder onto a new host after the extension was already removed
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the extension directory is live (not an archived/backup copy) and identify the browser profile owner. 2) CONTAIN: Force-remove the extension from Chrome and Edge, then verify no ExtensionInstallForcelist GPO/Intune policy or profile-sync will reinstall it; uninstalling clears its stored data. 3) HUNT: Cross-reference these hosts against the collector-callback UC; for any user who used ModHeader's header-history feature, rotate API keys, bearer tokens and session cookies, since full HTTP headers were stored on disk in plaintext.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "idgpnmonknjnojddfkpgkljpfnnfcklj"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Files=count(), SamplePath=any(FolderPath) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "idgpnmonknjnojddfkpgkljpfnnfcklj"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Files=count(), SamplePath=any(TargetFilePath) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName
| order by LastSeen desc

ModHeader browsing-history exfil POST to api.stanfordstudies.com/app/log AIActions on Objectives High
Targets the collector's activated exfiltration path specifically: an HTTP POST to api.stanfordstudies.com with the URI /app/log, which uploads the encrypted domain list plus device fingerprint before wiping the local copy. Requires web-proxy/gateway telemetry that captures URI and method, so it distinguishes real exfil from the dormant-state domain resolution. Rationale: The article and Yunus Aydın's teardown both name the exact upload target — a POST to api.stanfordstudies.com/app/log carrying the encrypted domain list and fingerprint — so matching host+method+URI on proxy logs is a high-fidelity signal that the dormant collector has actually been switched on. Cross-checked against: • https://aydinnyunus.github.io/2026/07/12/modheader-data-exfiltration-stanfordstudies/ • https://cyberpress.org/modheader-chrome-extension-exposes-900000/
ATT&CKT1567 T1041 T1082
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Benign traffic to an unrelated host that reuses the /app/log URI path on a different domain (host filter mitigates this)
  • Sandbox detonation of the sample generating the POST intentionally
  • A DLP/CASB solution replaying the request for inspection
  • Threat-intel tooling probing the endpoint for a live-verdict check
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the POST targeted api.stanfordstudies.com/app/log from a browser process and note SentBytes — a non-trivial body means the encrypted domain list was uploaded. 2) CONTAIN: Sinkhole/block stanfordstudies.com at DNS and proxy, remove the ModHeader extension from the host, and isolate if body size indicates bulk upload. 3) HUNT: This confirms the allow-list was populated (collector active) — sweep all hosts with the extension ID for the same POST, and rotate every secret (API keys, bearer tokens, session cookies) the affected users pasted into ModHeader's header-history feature, which stored full HTTP headers in plaintext on disk.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "api.stanfordstudies.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe", "msedge.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationHostName has "api.stanfordstudies.com" or RequestURL has "stanfordstudies.com"
| where RequestMethod == "POST" or RequestURL has "/app/log"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, SentBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] npm maintainer credential-phish lookalike domain npmjs.help (chalk/debug ATO)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — What is a dependency firewall?
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] plain-crypto-js postinstall RAT dropper spawns downloader (axios/Sapphire Sleet) · [LLM] axios RAT dropped artifacts: renamed PowerShell wt.exe + campaign 6202033 files · [LLM] axios RAT persistence: HKCU Run value MicrosoftUpdate pointing to system.bat · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] axios RAT C2 beacon to sfrclak[.]com / 142.11.206.73:8000 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Malicious postmark-mcp BCC email exfiltration to phan@giftshop[.]club · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
npm maintainer credential-phish lookalike domain npmjs.help (chalk/debug ATO) AIDelivery High
Hunts endpoint DNS/web contact to the lookalike domain npmjs.help, the fake '2FA reset' phishing site used to steal the npm maintainer credentials behind the September 2025 chalk/debug supply-chain compromise. Legitimate npm lives on npmjs.com/npmjs.org, so any hit on npmjs.help is a maintainer-targeted credential-phishing indicator. Rationale: npmjs.help is a confirmed lookalike phishing domain (registered 2025-09-05, three days pre-attack) named in the article and corroborated by Sygnia/Checkmarx/Cycode/Aikido as the credential-theft vector for the chalk/debug ATO. Exact-domain match against a domain with no legitimate use = high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/npm-debug-and-chalk-packages-compromised • https://www.sygnia.co/threat-reports-and-advisories/npm-supply-chain-attack-september-2025/ • https://checkmarx.com/zero-post/chalk-and-17-other-npm-packages-compromised-in-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1656
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC analyst or TI platform detonating/browsing npmjs.help in a sandboxed research VM
  • Automated URL-enrichment (SOAR/secure-web-gateway) resolving the domain for reputation scoring
  • Security-awareness phishing-simulation platform hosting a lookalike test page
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ appliance logging the blocked query
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host/user that resolved npmjs.help and whether a browser or npm tooling initiated it; pull any credential-entry or npm login activity in the following 30 min. 2) Contain: force-reset the affected npm account credentials and revoke/rotate npm publish tokens and 2FA; block npmjs.help at the proxy/DNS. 3) Hunt: check whether that maintainer published any npm package versions after the resolution timestamp, and scan lockfiles/CI for the chalk/debug malicious versions and browser-side crypto-address-swapping payloads.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "npmjs.help"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "npmjs.help"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

plain-crypto-js postinstall RAT dropper spawns downloader (axios/Sapphire Sleet) AIInstallation High
Hunts the malicious plain-crypto-js@4.2.1 postinstall (setup.js) hook — pulled in transitively by axios@1.14.1/0.30.4 — spawning a downloader/interpreter that references the RAT campaign artifacts (sfrclak C2, campaign ID 6202033) to fetch platform-specific payloads. Targets the exact execution behaviour Microsoft attributes to Sapphire Sleet. Rationale: sfrclak, 142.11.206.73, campaign ID 6202033 and the plain-crypto-js dependency name are Datadog/Elastic/Socket-confirmed IOCs for the March 2026 axios RAT dropper (setup.js postinstall). These strings do not appear in benign build output, making a command-line match high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/04/01/mitigating-the-axios-npm-supply-chain-compromise/ • https://socket.dev/blog/axios-npm-package-compromised

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
