  product: azure
  service: signinlogs
detection:
  selection:
    ResultType: 0
    AuthenticationProtocol: deviceCode
  condition: selection
level: medium
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success Authentication.signature="deviceCode" by Authentication.user Authentication.src_ip Authentication.app | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success Authentication.signature="deviceCode" by Authentication.user Authentication.src_ip Authentication.app | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Stolen M365 session token refresh — same account, many IPs, non-interactive (token aging) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the article's described behaviour of operators refreshing stolen tokens as they age out — the same corporate mailbox captured repeatedly from different IPs, and black-queen's autoRefresh tokens re-refreshed up to 25 times. Detects a single account accruing an abnormal number of distinct source IPs on non-interactive (refresh-token) sign-ins in a short window. Rationale: Directly models the article's 'repeated captures of the same accounts from different IPs' and autoRefresh tokens refreshed up to 25 times; non-interactive + high distinct-IP fan-out per account isolates token replay from normal user roaming. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/misconfigured-server-reveals-three.html • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1539
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Mobile users roaming across carrier/Wi-Fi networks generating many refresh IPs
  • Corporate VPN or SASE egress that rotates public IPs per session
  • Background Office/Outlook/Teams token refreshes across multiple devices for one power user
  • Shared service/kiosk account legitimately used from many locations
Suppression filter
| where not(Apps has_any ("Microsoft VPN Client","Microsoft Intune") )
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): review the IP/geo/ASN spread and app mix for the flagged account — legitimate roaming clusters by carrier/VPN ASN, whereas token theft shows unrelated hosting/VPS ASNs. Correlate against any interactive AiTM or device-code sign-in for the same user. Step 2 (contain): revoke all refresh tokens and sessions, reset credentials, and apply a short sign-in frequency + CAE-capable Conditional Access policy so a reset actually invalidates stolen tokens. Step 3 (hunt): enumerate mailbox rules, OAuth consents, and forwarding added during the window; check whether any of the fan-out IPs overlap the known Evilginx infra IPs and pivot to other victims.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| where IsInteractive == false
| summarize DistinctIPs=dcount(IPAddress), IPs=make_set(IPAddress,20), Countries=make_set(Country,20), Refreshes=count() by AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 1d)
| where DistinctIPs >= 5   // >=5 distinct refresh-token source IPs/day for one account = token-replay fan-out
| order by DistinctIPs desc
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == 0
| summarize DistinctIPs=dcount(IPAddress), IPs=make_set(IPAddress,20), Apps=make_set(AppDisplayName,20), Refreshes=count() by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1d)
| where DistinctIPs >= 5   // >=5 distinct refresh-token source IPs/day for one account = token-replay fan-out
| order by DistinctIPs desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` dc(Authentication.src_ip) as ip_count values(Authentication.src_ip) as src_ips count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success by Authentication.user _time span=1d | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where ip_count >= 5 | sort - ip_count
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(Authentication.src_ip) as ip_count values(Authentication.src_ip) as src_ips count from datamodel=Authentication where Authentication.action=success by Authentication.user _time span=1d | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where ip_count >= 5 | sort - ip_count
Endpoint connections to Evilginx phishing landing domains (picis.net / romnor.ca) AIDelivery High
Hunts managed endpoints resolving or connecting to the three phishing domains tied to the operations — picis[.]net and romnor[.]ca (plus queeenspropertyservices[.]ca) — which fronted the Evilginx AiTM proxies and their rotating wildcard subdomains. A hit means a user reached the phishing landing page and is a candidate victim before/at credential capture. Rationale: picis[.]net and romnor[.]ca are named as the two phishing domains and queeenspropertyservices[.]ca is in the IOC bundle; picis[.]net was still provisioning new subdomains as late as May 2026, so wildcard matching catches rotating hosts. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/misconfigured-server-reveals-three.html
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1557
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security analyst manually detonating the phishing URL from a corporate host during triage
  • Threat-intel sandbox/crawler VM resolving the domains for enrichment
  • URL-reputation or email-security appliance pre-fetching links from a managed endpoint
  • Domain later parked/reassigned to a benign owner after takedown, generating benign lookups
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): identify the user and process that made the request (browser vs automated tool) and whether a sign-in followed on the same identity shortly after (candidate AiTM capture). Step 2 (contain): sinkhole/block the three domains and their wildcards at DNS/proxy, and if the user authenticated, revoke sessions + reset credentials + re-register MFA. Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the resolved IPs (cross-check the four Evilginx infra IPs), search email/Safe Links telemetry for the delivering message and other recipients, and check for subsequent device-code or token-refresh anomalies on the affected account.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("picis.net","romnor.ca","queeenspropertyservices.ca")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("picis.net","romnor.ca","queeenspropertyservices.ca")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

ImFileEvent

                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",

           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

SecurityEvent

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

    object payload signature.

    - attack.t1059

    - attack.execution

    category: process_creation

            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'

            - '\mspub.exe'

            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High

| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent

AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018") or SHA1 in~ ("6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018") or MD5 in~ ("6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018") or SHA1 in~ ("6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018") or MD5 in~ ("6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["6a4cb1c75e1c59bbd4fbc4667f4c3bb5a74fe965", "2ea61cdead470f570586f513e22d43d787befec6", "35f23dfb4135d4cd38a6a29e64d79191d166344d", "eb8ede7598220dbef28953dc7df2e5418d52fa36", "f496736e2d2344de7963d4f722381f03227ec452", "cf3cbf93adf43d50618c88705857d3adb123ed24", "ea5d2096a2ef3dfe4fb870bd1f0270efaea993a6", "e9a44b3fe951cca57313533d6bc1d11e789c2018"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

iCagenda and Balbooa Forms Joomla Flaws Reportedly Exploited as Zero-Days

The Hacker News
2026-07-13 4 use cases 2 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added two maximum-severity security flaws impacting iCagenda and Balbooa extensions for Joomla to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, following reports of zero-day exploitation in the wild. The vulnerabilities, both rated 10.0 on the CVSS scoring system, are below - CVE-2026-48939 - A vulnerability in the

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] iCagenda 'Submit an Event' scanner UA 'icagenda-batch/1.0' in web logs (CVE-2026-48939)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] PHP web shell written to Joomla iCagenda/Balbooa upload folders (CVE-2026-48939, CVE-2026-56291)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] HTTP request to planted PHP shell under iCagenda/Balbooa upload paths (CVE-2026-48939, CVE-2026-56291)
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
iCagenda 'Submit an Event' scanner UA 'icagenda-batch/1.0' in web logs (CVE-2026-48939) AIDelivery High
Hunts web-server access logs for the automated exploitation scanner that identifies itself with the User-Agent 'icagenda-batch/1.0', the exact tool mySites.guru observed grabbing a token and POSTing a malicious upload to the iCagenda Submit-an-Event endpoint since 15 June 2026. This UA is not a legitimate browser, crawler or monitoring agent, so any hit is a direct exploitation attempt against CVE-2026-48939. Rationale: Uses the literal exploitation scanner UA 'icagenda-batch/1.0' named by mySites.guru and reproduced in the article; a non-browser UA string this specific has effectively zero legitimate use, making it alerting-grade on the first hit. Cross-checked against: • https://mysites.guru/blog/icagenda-zero-day-file-upload-rce/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-warns-of-actively-exploited-rce-flaws-in-joomla-extensions/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4rh3-rmh3-hv6h
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal vulnerability scanner (Nessus/Qualys) deliberately fingerprinting iCagenda with a spoofed UA during an authorized scan
  • Security researcher / red-team replaying the PoC against a staging site
  • A monitoring probe an admin scripted using the same UA string to test their own patch
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all requests from the matched source IP(s) — confirm the sequence token GET -> POST to the iCagenda submit endpoint -> GET of a new .php under images/icagenda/frontend/attachments/. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/edge and, if a PHP file was fetched, take the site offline or WAF-block the attachments path immediately. 3) Hunt: list images/icagenda/frontend/attachments/ for any .php/.phtml files, diff the Joomla #__users table for new Super Admin accounts, and confirm iCagenda is on 4.0.8/3.9.15.

PHP web shell written to Joomla iCagenda/Balbooa upload folders (CVE-2026-48939, CVE-2026-56291) AIInstallation High
Detects creation of a PHP-executable file inside the two upload directories these flaws write to — 'images/icagenda/frontend/attachments/' and 'images/baforms/uploads' — which by design should only ever hold user-submitted images and documents. A .php/.phtml/.phar in either folder is the planted web shell mySites.guru flagged as the primary IOC for both CVEs. Rationale: Pins on the two exact upload paths (images/icagenda/frontend/attachments/, images/baforms/uploads) plus PHP-executable extensions — both vendors explicitly say these folders must never contain PHP, so any hit is the planted shell rather than a legit attachment. Cross-checked against: • https://mysites.guru/blog/icagenda-zero-day-file-upload-rce/ • https://mysites.guru/blog/balbooa-forms-unauthenticated-file-upload-flaw/ • https://www.cycognito.com/blog/emerging-threat-cve-2026-56291-balbooa-forms-remote-code-execution-via-unauthenticated-file-upload/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Site migration/backup-restore tooling (Akeeba Kickstart, rsync) copying the whole webroot including an already-present benign file that happens to match
  • Admin manually placing a legitimate index.php as a directory-listing guard in the uploads folder
  • A previous compromise remediation that quarantined-in-place rather than deleting, retriggering on file rename
  • Antivirus renaming a detected file to .php.quarantine style names
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("kickstart.php","restore.php") and not (FolderPath has "backup" or FolderPath has "tmp\\install")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the dropped file — decode any eval/base64/assert/system calls, note the SHA256 and the InitiatingProcess (should be the web server / php-fpm). 2) Contain: delete/quarantine the file, WAF-block direct requests to the two upload paths, and isolate the host if the shell was already accessed. 3) Hunt: pull web logs for GET requests to that filename (attacker interaction), search for new Joomla Super Admin accounts and other recently-modified PHP files across the webroot, and confirm iCagenda>=4.0.8/3.9.15 and Balbooa Forms>=2.4.1.
DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed") | where FileName has_any (".php",".phtml",".phar",".php5") | where (FolderPath has "icagenda" and FolderPath has "attachments") or (FolderPath has "baforms" and FolderPath has "uploads") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256 | order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where TargetFileName has_any (".php",".phtml",".phar",".php5") | where (TargetFilePath has "icagenda" and TargetFilePath has "attachments") or (TargetFilePath has "baforms" and TargetFilePath has "uploads") | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername, TargetFileSHA256 | sort by TimeGenerated desc

HTTP request to planted PHP shell under iCagenda/Balbooa upload paths (CVE-2026-48939, CVE-2026-56291) AICommand & Control High
Detects the attacker fetching/executing the planted web shell — a GET/POST to a .php file located under 'images/icagenda/frontend/attachments/' or 'images/baforms/uploads' in web-server access logs. mySites.guru observed the scanner 'fetched the planted shell at the exact path the component writes attachments to', and requests to a PHP file in a media-upload directory are inherently anomalous. Rationale: Combines the two literal upload URI paths from both advisories with a '.php' request — a PHP file being requested from a media-attachment directory is the web-shell-interaction signal, distinct from the file-drop and the scanner-UA pivots. Cross-checked against: • https://mysites.guru/blog/icagenda-zero-day-file-upload-rce/ • https://mysites.guru/blog/balbooa-forms-unauthenticated-file-upload-flaw/ • https://www.securityweek.com/organizations-warned-of-exploited-joomla-extension-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate index.php directory-index guard in the uploads folder being requested by a crawler
  • Internal DAST/WAF validation scan probing the patched path and receiving a 404 (filter on scStatus==200 to cut these)
  • Uptime monitor configured to hit a known-good health-check PHP under a media path
Suppression filter
| where Status == 200
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the response status — a 200 to a .php in these folders means the shell executed; capture the source IP, requested filename and any query-string commands. 2) Contain: block the source IP and the upload path at the WAF, then delete the referenced PHP file from disk and isolate the web host. 3) Hunt: correlate the filename back to the DeviceFileEvents/FileWritten drop, review Joomla admin-user changes and outbound connections from the web host in the same window, and verify both extensions are patched.

jscrambler npm package publishes malicious preinstall binary

StepSecurity
2026-07-12 15 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

On July 11, 2026, version 8.14.0 of jscrambler was published to npm carrying a malicious preinstall hook that drops and executes a platform-specific native binary on Linux, Windows, and macOS. jscrambler is the official CLI client for the Jscrambler Code Integrity API, a commercial JavaScript obfuscation and web-app protection service, with a clean version history dating back to 0.1.0. The compromised release was flagged by StepSecurity's AI Release Analyzer with a suspicion score of 0 (the maximum suspicion rating) on publish.

Compromised jscrambler npm package (8.14.0+) artifacts written to node_modules AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for on-disk artifacts of the trojanized jscrambler npm release: the 7.8 MB dist/intro.js binary container written under node_modules/jscrambler and the extracted per-platform stealer payload hashes. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact package path, the disguised container file, and the three published payload SHA256s. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact IOC matrix: node_modules/jscrambler/dist/intro.js and the three extracted payload SHA256s. Corroborated by Socket.dev and The Hacker News, which confirmed the same package/path and Rust-compiled cross-platform stealer. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack • https://www.mallory.ai/stories/019f5225-a834-719b-9b66-c82edd147d7c

  • Threat-intel/EDR vendor test signatures replaying the same hashes
  • A cached copy of the tarball in an npm proxy/mirror directory being scanned
  • Internal malware-repo synchronization writing the sample to a lab share
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("malware-lab","sandbox","detonate"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is a developer/CI machine and check package-lock.json / node_modules for jscrambler at 8.14.0, 8.16.0, 8.17.0, 8.18.0 or 8.20.0 (all attacker-published). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill any process running from OS temp, downgrade to 8.13.0, and block the C2 IPs/domains. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for the extracted temp-dir binary, outbound Tor/C2 connections, and rotate every browser-stored credential, npm token (.npmrc), and cloud key used on that machine.

npm/node preinstall drops and executes hidden native binary from OS temp dir AIInstallation High
Hunts the core execution step: the jscrambler preinstall loader (dist/setup.js) decompresses a platform binary to a randomly named dotfile in the OS temp directory and launches it detached from the npm install tree. Detects node/npm spawning an executable whose path is a hidden dotfile under Temp or /tmp. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's loader behaviour: preinstall reads dist/intro.js and spawns a randomly named dotfile in the OS temp dir (.[a-z0-9]{6,} with .exe on Windows) detached from npm. Parent=node/npm + hidden temp binary is extremely rare in benign builds. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/jscrambler-npm-package-publishes-malicious-preinstall-binary • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1204.003 T1036.008
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legit native postinstall tools (esbuild, node-sass, sharp) extracting prebuilt binaries to temp — but those are not hidden dotfiles
  • node-based test harnesses that shell out to a scratch temp binary
  • Electron/pkg self-extracting apps unpacking to temp on first run
  • Yarn/pnpm build steps writing temp helper executables (rarely dotfiles)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("esbuild","node-sass","node-gyp","sharp","electron-builder"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the temp file path and SHA256, confirm parent is node/npm during an install window, and check if jscrambler 8.14.0+ is present. 2) Contain: kill the detached temp process, quarantine the temp binary, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: pull the process's outbound connections (Tor/C2 IPs), look for browser credential-store and .npmrc file access, and enumerate other hosts that installed the same package version.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","node")
| where FolderPath has_any ("Temp","/tmp/")
| where FileName startswith "."
| where FileName endswith ".exe" or FolderPath has "/tmp/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.exe")
| where NewProcessName has "Temp"
| extend LeafName = tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1])
| where LeafName startswith "." and LeafName endswith ".exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Execution of extracted jscrambler stealer payload by SHA256 AIInstallation Medium
Alerts on any process launched from one of the three published, extracted stealer payloads (ELF/PE32+/Mach-O) regardless of file name or drop path, catching the payload even if the loader randomizes its temp filename. Rationale: Uses the three exact payload SHA256s from the IOC table; hash-based execution detection survives the loader's random temp filename and is near-zero FP. Second-sourced as a Rust cross-platform infostealer by The Hacker News/Socket. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/jscrambler-npm-package-publishes-malicious-preinstall-binary • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html
ATT&CKT1204.003 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sandbox detonation of the sample by a malware analyst
  • EDR/AV backscan replaying the hash from quarantine
  • Threat-emulation exercise seeding the known-bad hash
Response runbook
1) Triage: this is a confirmed-malicious hash — verify the host, user context, and whether the binary already ran (child processes, network). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, quarantine, and begin credential rotation for all browser-stored secrets, npm tokens and cloud keys. 3) Hunt: enumerate every host in the org that installed jscrambler 8.14.0/8.16.0/8.17.0/8.18.0/8.20.0 and check for the same hash, temp dotfile, and C2 egress.

| where SHA256 in ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd","b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903","c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd","b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903","c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, ActingProcessName, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Stealer C2 egress to Tor Project infrastructure and hardcoded IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Detects outbound connections from a developer/CI host to the two hardcoded stealer C2 IPs and the check/archive.torproject.org endpoints the dropped binary contacts. High-fidelity because these are specific attacker-tied indicators, not generic Tor usage. Rationale: Uses the exact C2 IPs (37.27.122.124, 57.128.246.79) and torproject.org endpoints named in the Harden-Runner analysis and independently confirmed by second sources. Any dev host reaching these is high-signal for the stealer's C2. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/jscrambler-npm-package-publishes-malicious-preinstall-binary • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1090.003 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately running the Tor Browser or a Tor relay on their workstation (check.torproject.org is Tor's connectivity check)
  • Privacy-tooling test/QA reaching torproject.org
  • Security research replaying the C2 IPs in a lab
  • Threat-intel enrichment jobs actively probing the IOC IPs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tor.exe","firefox.exe","tor-browser.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — if it is a hidden temp binary or node/npm child during an install, treat as confirmed C2. 2) Contain: block the two IPs and torproject domains at the proxy/firewall, isolate the host, kill the process. 3) Hunt: correlate the connecting host to jscrambler 8.14.0+ installs, pull data-staging/exfil volume to those IPs, and rotate all credentials that could have been harvested.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("37.27.122.124","57.128.246.79")
   or RemoteUrl has_any ("check.torproject.org","archive.torproject.org")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("37.27.122.124","57.128.246.79")
   or DstHostname in~ ("check.torproject.org","archive.torproject.org")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

npm/node install spawns reconnaissance or shell utilities AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the preinstall execution phase where the compromised package's install context spawns local shells or host-recon tools — deviation from normal build behaviour. Reviewer-requested; grounded in the article's automatic preinstall-hook execution during npm install. Rationale: The article confirms the malicious code runs automatically via the npm preinstall hook; recon/download tools spawned by node/npm during install are anomalous for a JS-obfuscation CLI build and map to the stealer's discovery/staging behaviour reported by second sources (env/.npmrc/cloud-cred collection). Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/jscrambler-npm-package-publishes-malicious-preinstall-binary • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1087 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CI/CD build scripts that legitimately call curl/wget to fetch assets during install
  • node-based tooling invoking net.exe/reg.exe for environment setup
  • postinstall scripts running hostname/ipconfig for telemetry
  • cross-platform build tools shelling out to sh/uname on Linux runners
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild-install","electron","cypress","playwright install")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the parent npm/node command line and the package being installed; confirm whether jscrambler 8.14.0+ (or another unexpected package) is in the tree. 2) Contain: if unexpected, isolate the host and halt the CI job. 3) Hunt: pivot to any hidden temp binary spawned by the same node process, C2 egress, and access to .npmrc / browser credential stores.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","node","npm")
| where FileName in~ ("whoami.exe","systeminfo.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","hostname.exe","ipconfig.exe","reg.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe","whoami","hostname","id","uname","curl","wget")
| summarize ChildCount = dcount(FileName), Children = make_set(FileName), SampleCmd = any(ProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where ChildCount >= 1
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.exe")
| extend Child = tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1])
| where Child in~ ("whoami.exe","systeminfo.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","hostname.exe","ipconfig.exe","reg.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| summarize ChildCount = dcount(Child), Children = make_set(Child) by Computer, SubjectUserName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where ChildCount >= 1
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Persistence created by hidden temp-dir binary (scheduled task / Run key) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the stealer establishing persistence: a hidden binary running from the OS temp directory spawning schtasks.exe or writing a Run-key/registry autostart. Grounded in the article's temp-dotfile drop and corroborated persistence (Windows scheduled task / macOS LaunchAgent) reported by second sources. Rationale: Chains the article's temp-dotfile binary (from the IOC table) to the persistence step confirmed by second sources (Windows scheduled task / macOS LaunchAgent). Parent = hidden temp binary spawning schtasks/reg is a rare, high-fidelity persistence pivot distinct from the drop/exec UCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/jscrambler-npm-package-publishes-malicious-preinstall-binary • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-jscrambler-8140-npm-release.html
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate temp-extracted installer registering a scheduled task on first run
  • Software updaters writing a Run key from a temp staging binary
  • Admin scripting that creates scheduled tasks from a temp-located tool
  • EDR/RMM agents bootstrapping persistence from a temp path
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has_any ("Packages","WindowsApps","Program Files")
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the scheduled-task/Run-key target and the parent temp binary hash; confirm parent is a hidden dotfile. 2) Contain: delete the persistence entry, quarantine the temp binary, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: check for the payload SHA256, C2 egress to the known IPs/Tor domains, and jscrambler 8.14.0+ across the fleet; on macOS look for a matching LaunchAgent plist.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "Temp"
| extend ParentLeaf = tostring(split(InitiatingProcessFolderPath, "\\")[-1])
| where InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "."
| where (FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/create")
   or (FileName =~ "reg.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "Run")
   or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("New-ScheduledTask","CurrentVersion\\Run"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has "Temp"
| extend ParentLeaf = tostring(split(ParentProcessName, "\\")[-1])
| where ParentLeaf startswith "."
| extend Child = tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1])
| where (Child =~ "schtasks.exe" and CommandLine has "/create")
   or (Child =~ "reg.exe" and CommandLine has "Run")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

      - '\reg.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/create'
      - '\Run'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\Temp\\.*.exe) @Image:(*\\schtasks.exe OR *\\reg.exe) @CommandLine:(*create* OR *Run*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ParentImageFileName=/[\/\\]\.[a-z0-9]{6,}(\.exe)?$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(schtasks|reg)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/(\/create|\\Run)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentImageFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_path="*\\Temp\\.*" AND Processes.process_name IN ("schtasks.exe","reg.exe","powershell.exe") AND (Processes.process="*create*" OR Processes.process="*\\Run*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_path Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_path="*\\Temp\\.*" AND Processes.process_name IN ("schtasks.exe","reg.exe","powershell.exe") AND (Processes.process="*create*" OR Processes.process="*\\Run*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_path Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("37.27.122.124", "57.128.246.79") or RemoteUrl has_any ("")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["37.27.122.124", "57.128.246.79"]);

ImNetworkSession

   or Url has_any (BadDomains)

| order by TimeGenerated desc

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or SHA1 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd") or MD5 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd", "b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903", "c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Compromised jscrambler 8.14.0 npm Release Drops Rust Infostealer During Install

The Hacker News
2026-07-11 14 use cases 5 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The jscrambler npm package was compromised, and simply installing its&nbsp;8.14.0&nbsp;release runs an infostealer on your machine. Published on July 11, 2026, the malicious version carries a&nbsp;preinstall&nbsp;hook that drops and executes a native binary, one build each for Windows, macOS, and Linux. Socket flagged the release&nbsp;six minutes after it was published. If you or one of your

jscrambler 8.14.0 npm Package Installation AIDelivery High
Hunts for installation of the compromised jscrambler CLI npm package (8.14.0 and the sibling malicious versions 8.16.0/8.17.0/8.18.0/8.20.0 tied to the same actor) via npm/pnpm/yarn command lines on developer and CI hosts. Article-specific because it pins the exact package name and poisoned version window rather than generic npm abuse. Rationale: Anchors on the exact package name 'jscrambler' plus the poisoned version set from the article (8.14.0) enriched with the sibling malicious versions Socket attributed to the same actor. Version-pinned package name in an install command is very high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-backdoor-jscrambler-npm-package-with-infostealer-malware/
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A dependency-audit or SCA tool that echoes 'jscrambler@8.14.0' in its scan output command line
  • A remediation script explicitly uninstalling/overriding jscrambler@8.14.0 (npm uninstall / npm ls output)
  • A CI lockfile-pinning job that references the version string while forcing an upgrade to 8.15.0
  • A developer reproducing the incident in an isolated sandbox
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("uninstall","npm ls","npm audit","remove"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the command was an install (npm install/ci/add) not an uninstall/audit, and check whether the host is a build agent or developer laptop with access to cloud keys. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill any node.exe child processes, and remove jscrambler@8.14.0 from lockfiles/caches; pin to 8.13.0 or 8.15.0. 3) Hunt: on any confirmed install, treat all reachable secrets as stolen — rotate AWS/Azure/GCP keys, npm/GitHub tokens, and AI-tool/MCP API keys; pivot to UC2/UC3 to find the dropped binary and C2 callbacks.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe") or FileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "jscrambler" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("8.14.0","8.16.0","8.17.0","8.18.0","8.20.0")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "jscrambler" and CommandLine has_any ("8.14.0","8.16.0","8.17.0","8.18.0","8.20.0")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Rust Infostealer Binary Execution from npm Post-Install Hook AIInstallation High
Detects the setup.js preinstall loader (run by node.exe/npm) writing a hidden, randomly-named native binary into the system temp directory and executing it detached. Matches on the three published payload hashes and on the node→temp-hidden-executable parent/child chain specific to this campaign. Rationale: Uses the three published decompressed payload SHA-256 values plus the article's described chain (setup.js under node writes a hidden .{random}/.{random}.exe into temp and launches it detached). Hash match is deterministic; the behavioral clause catches recompiled variants. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-backdoor-jscrambler-npm-package-with-infostealer-malware/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate node-gyp / native-addon builds that write and run compiled binaries from temp during install
  • Electron or Puppeteer post-install steps that unpack helper binaries into temp
  • Test frameworks that spawn short-lived helper executables from a temp workspace
  • A developer's own build tool that emits dot-prefixed cache files in temp
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild","electron-builder") and SHA256 !in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd","b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903","c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: if a hash matches, this is confirmed malware — no further validation needed; for the behavioral hit, inspect the temp file name/signature and whether it was launched detached with hidden output. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the temp process tree, and capture the binary for the DFIR queue before AV quarantine removes it. 3) Hunt: pivot on the process ID into UC3 (C2 to 37.27.122.124 / 57.128.246.79), UC4 (credential file access), and UC5 (persistence) on the same host and across all CI agents that pulled jscrambler in the July 11+ window.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd","b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903","c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
   or (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe") and FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", "/tmp/", "/var/folders/") and FileName startswith ".")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in~ ("fbbcf4d8f98168f78f5c0c47a9ae56d59ec8ac84a7c9ca6b797fedfb8d62d2bd","b7ca95d1b23c8e67416a25cedf741de0917c2096bbc9d24649eea7853d054903","c8fd47d36bdf7c825378593ab82ed8c24d1dc52e26b507812393e24e1d5201fd")
   or (ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","npm.exe") and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\Temp\", "/tmp/", "/var/folders/"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

IronWorm C2 beacon to hardcoded jscrambler stealer IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any host reaching the two hard-coded attacker C2 IP addresses (37.27.122.124, 57.128.246.79) that StepSecurity observed the dropped jscrambler stealer contacting over TLS. Pure network-IOC pivot; independent of process telemetry so it catches the stealer even if EDR missed the drop. Rationale: Uses the two direct attacker C2 IPs StepSecurity published — the first network indicators for the campaign, confirmed across multiple write-ups. Static malicious IPs have essentially no legitimate business use. cloudwatch_query left empty: this is endpoint/firewall egress telemetry that does not live in CloudTrail, and VPC Flow fields fall outside the CloudTrail whitelist. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/jscrambler-supply-chain-attack • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-backdoor-jscrambler-npm-package-with-infostealer-malware/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A threat-intel enrichment or sandbox appliance deliberately connecting to the IOC IPs for analysis
  • A security researcher detonating the sample in a lab that shares the corporate egress
  • Shared cloud-provider IP reuse if the attacker infra is later reassigned (Hetzner/OVH ranges)
  • A vulnerability scanner probing the IPs as part of external attack-surface testing
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","malware-lab","detonation"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process on the host — if it maps to a temp-dropped hidden binary or node.exe child, escalate to confirmed stealer C2. 2) Contain: block 37.27.122.124 and 57.128.246.79 at the perimeter/EDR, isolate the source host, and snapshot memory. 3) Hunt: sweep all egress logs for these IPs and Tor bootstrap traffic (check.torproject.org / archive.torproject.org) from build agents; correlate to UC1 installs and rotate every secret reachable from that host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("37.27.122.124","57.128.246.79")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("37.27.122.124","57.128.246.79")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
